name: EDGI web-monitoring-db
purpose: Rails and PostgreSQL service that stores versions of monitored web pages, computes and serves diffs, and provides an annotation workflow for analysts to classify whether a change is substantive.
journalism_use_case: The newsroom-grade pipeline for monitoring thousands of government pages at once, with an annotation workflow so analysts can separate boilerplate churn from substantive policy rewording before anything reaches reporters — the capability that made EDGI's tracking of US environmental-policy page changes publishable.
pros: The analyst annotation workflow is the distinguishing feature and the reason this exists: at thousands of pages, the bottleneck is human triage, not detection, and no other tool here addresses it
Proven at exactly this scale by EDGI's own long-running government-page monitoring programme, which produced published findings — the most relevant provenance available
Uses the Internet Archive Wayback Machine as a version source, so you inherit historical coverage rather than only monitoring forward from today
Actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-13) with a clear separation between storage/annotation (this) and diffing (web-monitoring-diff)
cons: A multi-repository distributed system (db + ui + processing + diff + ops) that needs real engineering and ops capacity — the heaviest deployment in this subcategory and overkill below a few hundred monitored pages
GPL-3.0 copyleft is a constraint some newsroom legal teams will want to review, particularly if you expose a modified instance
It is a monitoring platform, not a notification tool: alerting and reporter-facing presentation are things you build around it
Small community (24 stars, 14 open issues) and no release objects, so operational support comes from reading the code and EDGI's documentation
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The documented provenance is strong: EDGI operates a public instance and has used this stack for sustained government-page monitoring with published outputs. 24 stars, 14 open issues, last push 2026-11-13, no releases.
assessment: The right answer when monitoring becomes a programme rather than a few watches — and for an outlet tracking state rewriting of official records, that threshold arrives quickly. For your profile I would scope it as a project with named analyst capacity, because deploying it without people to work the annotation queue reproduces the problem it solves. Pair with web-monitoring-diff and keep the version source pointed at Wayback so you get history for free.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-13, no release objects, 24 stars, 14 open issues. Current commits from an organisation that operates the software publicly; small community but demonstrably in production use.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Page versions sourced from the Internet Archive are subject to IA's terms and the original publishers' rights.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0: distributing a modified version obliges source release; hosting a modified instance for third parties is the case to review with legal counsel.
costs: No software fee. Infrastructure estimate: Rails app servers, PostgreSQL sized to version storage (which grows with page count × capture frequency), Redis/Sidekiq workers, plus the diff service — realistically several VMs and meaningful storage for thousands of pages. Dominant cost is analyst time working the annotation queue. Assumptions: self-hosted, Wayback as version source.
privacy: Page versions, diffs and analyst annotations are held in your own PostgreSQL database. EDGI's public instance is a separate deployment. Monitoring public government pages raises no subject-privacy issue; your watch list does reveal editorial priorities, so protect the instance accordingly.
alternatives: changedetection.io for a far lighter deployment below the triage threshold
web-monitoring-diff alone if you have your own storage and only need diffs
Klaxon for reporter-driven rather than analyst-driven monitoring
summary: Rails and PostgreSQL service that stores versions of monitored web pages, computes and serves diffs…

name: EDGI web-monitoring-diff
purpose: Python library and optional HTTP service providing multiple diff algorithms for web content — HTML source, rendered text, links, and side-by-side visual comparison — tuned for comparing archived captures.
journalism_use_case: Produces the side-by-side and inline HTML diffs that let a reporter see exactly which sentences, links or data tables were removed from an official page between two archived captures — the artefact that turns 'the page changed' into a publishable finding.
pros: Multiple diff types (source, text, links) let you ask different questions: a removed link to a dataset is a different story from reworded guidance, and link diffing surfaces quiet removals that text diffing misses
Purpose-built for archived government pages rather than generic text, so it handles the templating realities of agency sites better than off-the-shelf diff
Usable as a library or an HTTP endpoint, so it integrates into either a pipeline or a platform
Actively released (v0.3.0, 2026-11-13, same-day push) and deliberately decoupled from the storage platform
cons: A component rather than a product: no scheduling, storage, alerting or UI, so it only earns its place inside a larger system you build or run
HTML diffing of heavily templated government pages still needs filtering to suppress navigation, timestamp and session noise — the library helps but does not solve this, and tuning is per-site work
GPL-3.0 copyleft affects redistribution inside a product
47 open issues against 26 stars — a high ratio indicating known rough edges in a small project
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: release v0.3.0 on 2026-11-13 with same-day push; 26 stars with 47 open issues. In production use behind EDGI's own monitoring programme, which is verifiable from the sibling repository's configuration.
assessment: Worth adopting as the diffing layer whenever you build monitoring yourself, because the link-diff capability in particular catches removals that text diffs hide — and quiet removal of a dataset link is a recurring story. Budget per-site filtering work; that is the real cost and it is unavoidable with any HTML diffing approach. Pair with web-monitoring-db for storage and triage, or with your own capture pipeline.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-13, latest release v0.3.0 published the same day, 26 stars, 47 open issues. Current releases under institutional maintenance; the backlog reflects the difficulty of HTML diffing rather than neglect.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0: embedding in a distributed product triggers source-release obligations. Internal use unaffected.
costs: No fee. Processes content in memory or over a local HTTP endpoint; negligible infrastructure. Cost is engineer time on per-site noise filtering.
privacy: Processes content in memory or over a local HTTP endpoint with no outbound data flows of its own — one of the cleanest privacy profiles in this segment.
alternatives: Standard diff tooling plus html2text for simpler needs
changedetection.io's built-in diffing if you use that platform
git-based diffing via shot-scraper for a lighter approach
summary: Python library and optional HTTP service providing multiple diff algorithms for web content — HTML source, rendered text, links…

name: wayback (Python client for the Internet Archive Wayback Machine)
purpose: Python client for the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine CDX and Memento endpoints, enumerating captures of a URL and retrieving the exact archived bytes for a given timestamp.
journalism_use_case: Enumerate every archived capture of a government URL and pull the exact bytes of two dates to prove what a page said before and after an edit — without screen-scraping the Wayback web interface, which breaks and is unreliable at scale.
pros: Gives you the exact archived bytes rather than a rendered screenshot, which is what you need for a defensible before-and-after comparison
Proper CDX enumeration means you can find the captures that exist rather than guessing dates — the step most manual Wayback research gets wrong
BSD-3-Clause, well documented, actively released (v0.5.1, 2026-06-19) by the team that uses it in production monitoring
Turns a third-party archive into a programmable evidence source, which is extremely cost-effective compared with running your own crawls retrospectively
cons: Only as good as the Internet Archive's crawl coverage: pages never captured, captured rarely, or excluded by robots or takedown cannot be reconstructed — and coverage of non-Western government sites is notably thin
No diffing, scheduling or alerting of its own; it is an access library
Your query pattern is visible to the Internet Archive, so enumerating captures of a specific target discloses your interest to a third party
Small community (94 stars, 25 open issues), and IA endpoint behaviour and rate limits can change outside your control
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: release v0.5.1 (2026-06-19), last push 2026-11-06, 94 stars with 25 open issues; in production use within EDGI's monitoring stack. Internet Archive coverage limitations are a well-documented general property of web archiving rather than a defect of this client.
assessment: Adopt it — the cost-benefit is excellent, because it lets you reconstruct history you never captured yourself. Two disciplines for your work: treat absence of captures as absence of evidence rather than evidence of no change, and start your own forward capture (Scoop, ArchiveBox) for any target that matters, because relying solely on IA means your evidence depends on someone else's crawler and someone else's takedown policy.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-06, latest release v0.5.1 (2026-06-19), 94 stars, 25 open issues. Regular releases under institutional maintenance with production use behind EDGI's monitoring.
model_or_data_licence: Archived content belongs to the original publishers; Internet Archive access terms apply to retrieval.
licence_restrictions: None material for the client. Republishing archived content raises the original publisher's rights, which is a separate editorial/legal judgement.
costs: No fee. Negligible compute. The Internet Archive is a free service; heavy querying should be rate-limited out of courtesy rather than cost.
privacy: Sends the URLs you query to the Internet Archive and pulls archived content back, so your query pattern — which targets you are researching — is visible to IA. Consider this when researching a sensitive target.
alternatives: waybackpack or waybackpy as alternative Python clients
Scoop or ArchiveBox for forward capture under your own control
pywb to serve your own captures alongside IA material
summary: Python client for the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine CDX and Memento endpoints…

name: shot-scraper
purpose: CLI wrapper over Playwright that takes screenshots of web pages, extracts content by executing JavaScript against them, and is designed to be driven from YAML configuration in CI.
journalism_use_case: Run a scheduled job that screenshots or extracts a government page and commits the result to Git, turning every quiet edit into a dated, diffable commit you can point at in a story — a monitoring system built from a CLI, a repository and a cron schedule.
pros: The git-commit-as-monitoring pattern is elegant and cheap: version history gives you dated evidence, diffs and an audit trail with no bespoke platform
JavaScript extraction means you can pull a specific value (a number from a dashboard, a row from a table) and commit that, making the diff semantically meaningful rather than pixel noise
Apache-2.0, actively released (1.12, 2026-09-13), excellent documentation, and composes naturally with git-history and Datasette for querying the time series
Trivial to run in GitHub Actions or any CI, so there is no server to operate
cons: No notification or diff-review layer — you assemble alerting yourself from git tooling or CI, which is fine for an engineer and a barrier for anyone else
Requires comfort with YAML, Git and CI, so it is not a reporter-facing tool
Screenshots alone are not text-diffable, so you must pair them with JavaScript or text extraction to get meaningful diffs — a design decision people get wrong initially
If the monitoring repository is public, the monitored URLs and captured content become public, which can disclose an investigation's targets
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 2,609 stars with 63 open issues, release 1.12 (2026-09-13), last push 2026-10-14. The git-commit monitoring pattern is documented by the maintainer and widely used alongside Datasette tooling in data-journalism contexts.
assessment: My preferred lightweight monitoring approach for an engineer-led team, because the evidence artefact (a git history) is simultaneously the audit trail and the alerting substrate. For your profile the one rule that matters: keep the monitoring repository private unless you intend your targets to be public, since a public repo of watched URLs is a map of your investigations. Add text extraction alongside screenshots so diffs are readable.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-14, latest release 1.12 (2026-09-13), 2,609 stars, 63 open issues. Regular releases from a maintainer with a strong track record of long-term project care.
costs: No fee. CI minutes if run in GitHub Actions (free tier is usually sufficient for modest schedules; current limits not verified here) or a small host. Playwright browser downloads add disk. Negligible.
privacy: Outputs land in your repository or local disk. The critical consideration is repository visibility: if the repo is public, the monitored URLs and captured content become public. Private repositories keep both internal.
alternatives: changedetection.io for a UI and built-in alerting
webchanges for CLI monitoring with notification backends included
Scoop where you need provenance-attested single-page captures rather than a time series
summary: CLI wrapper over Playwright that takes screenshots of web pages, extracts content by executing JavaScript against them…

name: Awesome Website Change Monitoring
purpose: Curated list of website change-monitoring tools and services, open-source and commercial, with a linked comparison spreadsheet.
journalism_use_case: The fastest way for a newsroom to see what monitoring options exist and which are abandoned before committing engineering time, and where commercial alternatives such as Fluxguard/Versionista, VisualPing, Wachete and PageFreezer are catalogued alongside open-source options.
pros: Covers commercial services alongside open-source tools, which is useful because the honest answer for some newsrooms is a paid service rather than a self-hosted deployment
CC0-1.0, so you can copy and adapt it into internal documentation without any licence consideration
Maintained by an organisation that actually runs monitoring at scale, so the curation reflects practical experience
Points to a deeper comparison spreadsheet with feature-level detail that a README cannot carry
cons: Several entries are stale or unmaintained (NewsDiffs, NYTdiff, DiffEngine, Pagelyzer) and the list does not flag that — so it can send you toward dead tools, which this catalogue corrects
Omits generalist tools journalists now often use, notably urlwatch, webchanges and the git-plus-screenshot pattern
The substantive comparison lives in an external Google Spreadsheet linked from the README, so the authoritative content is not version-controlled with the list
A list, not a tool: 515 stars and 16 open issues, last push 2026-08-11
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: CC0-1.0 licence; last push 2026-08-11; 515 stars with 16 open issues. The staleness of several listed entries was verified independently in this catalogue — diffengine (last release 2020) and NewsDiffs (default branch last commit 2018) are both listed without deprecation notes.
assessment: Useful as a starting map, with the caveat that it does not distinguish live from dead. Read it alongside this catalogue's maintenance classifications rather than on its own. The genuinely valuable part for your profile is the commercial-service coverage: if your newsroom lacks ops capacity, a paid monitoring service may be the correct answer, and this list is the fastest way to see the field.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-08-11, no releases, 515 stars, 16 open issues. Three months since last push; a curated list updated episodically. Not declining, but entries have demonstrably aged without being marked.
model_or_data_licence: CC0-1.0 — public domain dedication, so free to copy into internal docs.
costs: None to read. Note that the commercial services it catalogues have their own pricing, none of which was verified in this survey.
privacy: No software and no data flows. The deeper comparison lives in an external Google Spreadsheet, so opening it discloses your interest to Google in the ordinary way.
alternatives: This catalogue's B1 segment for maintenance-verified assessments
changedetection.io or webchanges if you have already decided to self-host
summary: Curated list of website change-monitoring tools and services, open-source and commercial, with a linked comparison spreadsheet

name: diffengine
maintainer: Documenting the Now (DocNow; transferred from edsu)
purpose: Tool that watches RSS/Atom feeds, detects when article text changes after publication, generates a visual diff image, archives the versions to the Internet Archive and posts the diff to social media.
journalism_use_case: The reference design for publicly surfacing stealth edits to anything with a feed — news sites, ministry press-release feeds, agency blogs — with an Internet Archive snapshot attached to each detected change, making the before state independently verifiable.
pros: The design pattern is genuinely good: feed-driven detection, visual diff, third-party archive snapshot, public posting — each step reinforces the evidentiary value of the next
Attaching an Internet Archive snapshot per change means the before state is attested by a third party, not just your local cache
MIT licensed, and the repository transfer from edsu to DocNow is confirmed by redirect, so the lineage is traceable
cons: Unmaintained since 2020: last push 2020-06-25 and release v0.2.7 (2020-09-30), with 30 open issues — six years untouched
Social integration is broken by default because it was built for a Twitter API that no longer works as assumed, so the publishing half of the design is dead
Aged browser-automation dependencies (GeckoDriver/Firefox) and an old Python stack make installation a project in itself
Only monitors content reachable through a feed, so pages without RSS/Atom are out of scope
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: last push 2020-06-25, release v0.2.7 (2020-09-30), 182 stars, 30 open issues; repository transfer edsu → DocNow confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17. Its social-posting dependency on the old Twitter API is the clearest cause of obsolescence.
assessment: Reference only, but the design is worth stealing. For your profile, rebuild the pattern with current components: feedparser or a direct feed poller for detection, web-monitoring-diff for the diff, Scoop or the IA save endpoint for the snapshot, and an internal channel rather than a social platform for the notification. That gets you diffengine's evidentiary chain on maintained foundations in a day or two.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2020-06-25, latest release v0.2.7 (2020-09-30), 182 stars, 30 open issues. Six years without activity and a core integration (Twitter API) that no longer exists as assumed. No deprecation notice, hence dormant rather than archived.
licence_restrictions: None, but the code is effectively frozen.
costs: No fee. Not worth operating as-is given dependency age.
privacy: Diffs stored locally, but the design is deliberately public: snapshots go to the Internet Archive and diff images were posted to social media. If you rebuild the pattern, decide consciously whether publication is wanted — for monitoring a target during an active investigation it is not.
alternatives: webchanges or changedetection.io for maintained feed and page monitoring
web-monitoring-diff plus the IA save endpoint to reproduce the evidentiary chain
NewsDiffs — also dormant; see its entry
blockers: Unmaintained since 2020; social integration depends on a withdrawn Twitter API
summary: Tool that watches RSS/Atom feeds, detects when article text changes after publication, generates a visual diff image…

name: NewsDiffs
purpose: Django application that scrapes news articles from configured sites on a schedule, stores every version, and publishes a public archive of detected post-publication edits.
journalism_use_case: The canonical prior art for stealth-edit tracking and a useful reference for how to structure per-site parsers and a public diff archive — not a tool to deploy today, but the project that established the practice of holding news organisations accountable for silent revisions.
pros: Historically important: it demonstrated that systematic post-publication edit tracking is feasible and newsworthy, and the public-archive model shaped later work
Per-site parser architecture is a reasonable design for the problem, and reading it saves you rediscovering the same structure
506 stars reflect genuine historical influence in this space
cons: Effectively abandoned: the last default-branch commit dates to 2018 and the stack targets Python 2.6+ with old Django versions — an end-of-life runtime that cannot be deployed safely
GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION, and session-1 inspection found mixed per-file licensing, so reuse needs file-by-file review
The README itself notes you must be a programmer to add a parser for each new site, so it never scaled beyond its curators
36 open issues, no releases; the public site's continuity is outside your control
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: last default-branch commit 2018 (with a 2026-04-13 push reflecting incidental repository activity rather than development), Python 2.6+ requirement, mixed per-file licensing and SPDX NOASSERTION, 506 stars with 36 open issues.
assessment: Reference only, and specifically a cautionary one: per-site scrapers are a maintenance treadmill, which is why this project stopped. For your profile the lesson is to prefer feed- or sitemap-driven detection and generic diffing over bespoke parsers, and to accept lower coverage in exchange for a system that survives. If post-publication edit tracking matters to your beat, build it on webchanges or shot-scraper with a sitemap crawl rather than reviving this.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-04-13 but the default-branch development history ends in 2018; no releases, SPDX NOASSERTION, 506 stars, 36 open issues. Python 2.6+ and old Django make it non-deployable. The recent push date is misleading and is the reason push recency alone is not used for classification in this catalogue.
licence: MIT per session-1 inspection, but mixed per-file licensing was found and GitHub reports NOASSERTION — reuse requires file-by-file review
licence_restrictions: Unclear in aggregate. Do not vendor code from it without reviewing each file's header.
costs: No fee. Not deployable on a supported runtime without substantial porting work.
privacy: Self-hosted; the original project published detected diffs publicly on its own website. A revival would need an explicit decision about publication.
alternatives: webchanges or changedetection.io for maintained monitoring
shot-scraper plus git for a version history of specific articles
EDGI web-monitoring-db for a platform with analyst triage
blockers: Python 2.6-era stack, abandoned since 2018, mixed per-file licensing
summary: Django application that scrapes news articles from configured sites on a schedule, stores every version…

name: DataIndex.us (Federal Data Terminations Tracker)
purpose: Hosted tracker documenting US federal datasets that have been terminated, altered or had variables removed, plus pending changes to statistical collections, with an email newsletter.
journalism_use_case: Check whether a federal dataset you are about to rely on has been terminated, altered or had variables removed — and pick up story leads from documented removals and pending collection changes. For reporting that depends on official statistics, this is a direct check on whether the ground has moved under a story.
pros: Addresses a real and under-covered problem: datasets disappear or change definition quietly, and a story built on last year's variable can be silently wrong
Curated by a credible policy organisation with subject expertise, so entries carry context rather than just diffs
Zero effort to use — a reporter reads the site or subscribes to the newsletter
Documented removals are themselves story leads, not just defensive checks
cons: Despite the site's statement that its code is GPL v3, no public repository was found in this survey, so it cannot be verified as open-source software or self-hosted — treat it as a hosted dataset and dashboard
Scope is US federal data only, so it does not help for other jurisdictions
As a hosted third-party service it carries continuity risk: if it stops, the historical record of what was removed may not be preserved elsewhere
Licence and terms unverified, so you should link to it rather than republish its contents as a dataset
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: no public repository was found during this survey despite the site's GPL v3 code statement — verified by search on 2026-11-17 and recorded as unresolved. The service is live with a newsletter.
assessment: Worth adding to your routine as a pre-flight check whenever a story leans on US federal statistics, and worth subscribing to for leads. But treat it as a secondary source: when a removal matters to a story, corroborate against the agency's own site, the Federal Register notice, and an archived capture (Wayback or your own), and cite those. Also note the dependency asymmetry — a tracker of disappearing data that itself disappears is a known failure mode, so capture pages you rely on.
maintenance_evidence: No public repository found in this survey, so repository-based assessment is impossible. The hosted site and newsletter were live as of this survey. Classified Uncertain because a hosted service's maintenance cannot be evidenced the way a repository's can, and the claimed open-source code could not be located.
licence: Not verified — the site states its code is GPL v3 but no public repository was found; terms of use for the data were not verified
model_or_data_licence: Not verified. Underlying federal sources are generally US government works (public domain in the US), but FAS's compilation and annotations may carry their own rights.
licence_restrictions: Unverified. Link and cite rather than republishing the compilation as a dataset.
costs: Free to read; newsletter free. No infrastructure. Not self-hostable in practice.
privacy: Journalists read from the hosted site or email newsletter; no local data holding and no measurement. Subscribing discloses your interest and email address to FAS.
alternatives: EDGI web-monitoring-db for systematic self-hosted monitoring of agency pages and datasets
Your own changedetection.io or webchanges watches on the specific dataset landing pages you depend on
Internet Archive captures plus the wayback client for reconstructing what a dataset page said
blockers: No public repository located; licence and terms unverified; hosted single point of failure
summary: Hosted tracker documenting US federal datasets that have been terminated, altered or had variables removed…
oss_detail: Hosted service or proprietary software — governed by service terms, not a software licence
